introduction.title: What the Rack Pull Is For
paragraphs: A rack pull is a deadlift that starts from pins or blocks instead of the floor, usually with the bar just below the knees. The shorter range of motion lets you handle more weight than your deadlift, which builds the upper back, traps and hip extensors that lock out a heavy pull.

It also gets you comfortable with heavy weight in your hands. Many lifters use rack pulls alongside the deadlift, and some use them to keep pulling heavy through a stretch when a full range deadlift does not suit them.

faqItems.question: How high should the pins be for rack pulls?
faqItems.answer: Just below the knee is the most common height, because it keeps your body position close to the middle of a real deadlift. Pulls from above the knee let you lift far more weight but look much less like the deadlift you want to improve.

faqItems.question: Do rack pulls improve your deadlift?

faqItems.question: How much more can I rack pull than deadlift?
faqItems.answer: From just below the knee, many lifters rack pull around 10 percent more than their deadlift, and higher pins allow more. The size of the gap is useful information: a large one often means the floor portion of your deadlift has room to grow.

faqItems.question: Should I use straps for rack pulls?
faqItems.answer: Straps are a sensible choice for heavy rack pulls. The goal is to load your back and hips with more than you can deadlift, and that weight will often outrun your grip.

faqItems.question: Are rack pulls easier on the back than deadlifts?
faqItems.answer: The shorter range means less distance under load on each rep, but the weights are heavier. Keep your back flat and the reps controlled, and give heavy rack pulls the same care as a heavy deadlift.

faqItems.question: How often should I do rack pulls?
faqItems.answer: Once a week is plenty for most lifters, usually on a pulling day alongside or in place of lighter deadlifts.
